title: The two of us — dvojina
goal: Install Slovenian's most distinctive feature: the form for EXACTLY TWO. After this unit you won't be able to mention two people without pausing to count — and that's precisely the point.
bekal: choose *-va* or *-ve* according to the pair's gender, and know why the masculine always wins

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Zakaj "greva", ne "gremo"?
dialogs.intro: Outside the lecture building. Maja arrives with her friend Eva. Budi gets a grammar lesson he didn't ask for.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Živjo, Budi! To je Eva. Midve sva sošolki.
lines.id: Hi, Budi! This is Eva. We're classmates.
lines.literal: hi, Budi! this is Eva. we-two-f are classmates-two-f.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Me veseli, Eva. Vidve sta iz Ljubljane?
lines.id: Nice to meet you, Eva. Are you two from Ljubljana?
lines.literal: me pleases, Eva. you-two-f are from Ljubljana?

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Jaz sem iz Ljubljane, Maja pa iz Kopra.
lines.id: I'm from Ljubljana, and Maja's from Koper.
lines.literal: I am from Ljubljana, Maja but from Koper.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I see. And what are you two doing today?

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Greva na kavo. Greš z nama?
lines.id: We're going for coffee. Want to come with us?
lines.literal: we-two-go to coffee. you-go with us-two?

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Ker sva dve. Za tri je "gremo".
lines.id: Because we're two. For three it's "gremo".
lines.literal: because we-two-are two-f. for three is "we-go".

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: In če grem zraven, smo trije?
lines.id: So if I come along, we're three?
lines.literal: and if I-go along, we-are three-m?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Torej dvojina umre, ko pride tretji.
lines.id: So the dual dies as soon as a third person arrives.
lines.literal: so dual dies, when comes third.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.id: That's why it's so romantic. Let's go!

notes: **Midve, not midva — because both are women.** Slovenian sorts pairs by gender: **midve** when both are women, **midva** for everything else. "Everything else" means two men *and also* one man with one woman. In a mixed pair the masculine form wins — the same rule holds across the Slavic languages, and Slovenians themselves have long joked about it.

**Dvojina is not a style choice.** Saying *mi smo* for two people isn't "a bit sloppy", it's wrong — like saying "all three of us" while pointing at two people. So every time you're about to mention more than one person, Slovenian makes you **count first**. That habit is what this unit is really about.

**The nouns change too, not just the verbs.** Look at *sošolki* in the first line: it's not *sošolka* (one) or *sošolke* (three or more), but the dual form. The same happens with adjectives: *lepa hiša* (one beautiful house), *lepi hiši* (two beautiful houses), *lepe hiše* (three or more beautiful houses).

**Z nama = "with the two of us".** Dual pronouns have their own form for each case, and *nama* is one of them. Don't memorize the table now; memorize the three chunks you'll use most: *z nama* (with us two), *z vama* (with you two), *naju* (us two, as the object).

**Trije, not tri.** Even numbers have gender in Slovenian: *trije* for masculine, *tri* for feminine and things. Likewise *dva* versus *dve*. The number system is taken apart fully in unit 5; for now, just know that Slovenian numbers aren't entirely neutral.

grammars.title: Dvojina — three lanes, not two
body: This is the table that sets Slovenian apart from some seven thousand other languages. The middle column is what English, most European languages, and every Slavic language lack — except for Slovenian's little cousin in eastern Germany.
after: The sound rule is very simple: **swap the plural ending *-mo* for *-va***, and you have the dual form for "we two". For "you two" and "they two", swap *-te* or *-jo* for **-ta**.
Since *vidva* and *onadva* share the same verb form (*sta*, *govorita*, *delata*), you really only need to learn **two** new endings: *-va* and *-ta*. That's the whole cost of the dual in verbs.

grammars.title: Nouns in the dual
body: Nouns have their own form for two as well. This table uses all three Slovenian noun genders at once — masculine, feminine, and neuter — which get taken apart fully in unit 4.
after: The pattern: masculine words add **-a**, feminine and neuter words add **-i**. Three lines to memorize, and most A1 nouns are covered.

Watch out for one neat trap: *brata* can mean "two brothers" (dual) **or** "of a brother" (Genitive singular, like *iz Maribora*). The forms are twins. Only the sentence tells them apart — *Imam brata* = "I have a brother", while *Brata sta doma* = "The two brothers are at home". The verb gives away which one is meant.

grammars.title: Oba in obe — "both"
body: A word that lives only inside the dual, and one you'll need often once you start talking about two people.

head: Form
Say it
Used for
Example
rows: *Oba sta doma.* — Both are at home.
*Obe sestri sta študentki.* — Both sisters are students.

after: *Oba* and *obe* are used just like English "both", but they pull in a dual verb: *Oba sta* — not *Oba so*.
If you want to stress that two people do something **together**, add *skupaj*: *Greva skupaj* = "We're going together".

blocks.text: Family is where the dual shows up most in everyday conversation — there are two parents, two pairs of grandparents, and a couple is, by definition, two.

Look at **starši** (parents): it has no singular and no dual form — it's always plural, even though there are clearly two people. Slovenian treats them as one group, not a pair. If you want to stress both of them, use *oba starša*.

Note too that, like English, Slovenian doesn't have separate everyday words for older and younger siblings. *Brat* means brother, whatever his age. If you need to be precise: *starejši brat* (older brother), *mlajši brat* (younger brother).

head: Sentence
Say it
Meaning
rows: I have a brother and a sister.
Both my parents are at home.
The two of us are married.

sections.title: Why Slovenians are proud of the dual

blocks.text: In Slovenia the dual isn't just a grammar footnote; it's part of how people tell the story of who they are. T-shirts, greeting cards, and tourism posters use it as a national in-joke, and the joke is always the same: their language has a special form for **a pair**.
The sentence *Midva sva* — two words — already announces that exactly two people are speaking, no more and no less. English needs *the two of us*. Slovenian has already settled it in the verb ending.

head: Sentence
Say it
Meaning
rows: Shall we two go for a drink?
What are you two up to?

blocks.text: Look at *Se vidiva* and *Se slišiva*: the two most common goodbyes in Slovenia, and both are dual — because the people parting are two, you and the person you're talking to. If you say goodbye to three friends at once, they become *Se vidimo* and *Se slišimo*.

blocks.title: A habit to install now
items: Before mentioning more than one person, stop for half a second and **count**. Two? Use *-va* or *-ta*. Three or more? Only then *-mo*, *-te*, *-jo*.
That half second feels awkward for two weeks, then it disappears. After that you choose the form without noticing — and from then on, Slovenians stop hearing the most glaring mistake foreigners make.
Mi smo iz Ljubljane. (two people, at least one male)
